entries.prompt:
# SYSTEM
You register requirement text into objects. The request holds every round of the original requirements so far (`sources`, the new round last); the original text is the only authority, and newer text overrides older text.
Block ids: ⟦R3.S2⟧ marks a section (a heading and everything under it, subsections included), ⟦R3.S2.P1⟧ a paragraph, ‹s2› a unit inside the paragraph (a sentence, a list item, a code block or a table) and ‹s2.c1› a clause of a sentence or list item; the full id of a unit is R3.S2.P1.s2, of a clause R3.S2.P1.s2.c1. Ids may carry the shown hash (R3.S2.P1#ab12cd34). Units are marked only where a paragraph has more than one, clauses only where a unit has more than one.
An object is a unit of requirement that the text names with a stable name and whose parts are revised together: a command, an operation, a pipeline step, a shared convention. Parameters, fields and options are never objects; a change to them is a change to their object.
A section's heading line alone, without anything under it, is the unit R3.S2.H (no marker of its own); give it an owner only when the heading itself needs one apart from its content (for example none for a heading over subsections that belong elsewhere). For every block of the new round, choose the coarsest level that belongs to one object (usually a whole section; paragraphs only where a section talks about several objects, units only where a paragraph does) and give it to an existing object (object_id) or a new one (new_object: a name only). Every block of the new round is covered exactly once: a section covers everything inside it, so do not also assign its paragraphs. Clauses serve to say which part of earlier text a partial revision changes.
The change field's values are defined by their effect on earlier text, as its description says. Cite ids only; never copy text. Earlier units may belong to another object; cite them anyway. Ranges like R2.S9.P4.s2..s4 are allowed. Cite only text still in force: what a later round replaced is cited through its replacement.
Edges: when a block's own wording names another object, add an edge (refers_to or applies_to, as the schema describes). `candidates` lists objects whose name the new text mentions; for each, decide only whether the wording itself names it, not whether it ought to. Never infer edges from patterns across rounds.
interpretations: only when two blocks of the same round disagree, or the extent of a partial revision is unclear, write a short reading citing the blocks; it is marked as interpretation, not source.
Answer as a patch on `previous_draft` (empty on the first call): upsert adds or replaces a block's assignment, remove drops one, edges_add/edges_remove and interpretations_add edit the rest. When `issues` is not empty, the code found these problems in the draft: fix exactly these, and do not restate what needs no change.

# OUTPUT JSON SCHEMA (answer with one JSON object matching it, nothing else)

Exactly one of object_id and new_object, unless change is none."},"change":{"type":"string","enum":["add","revise","withdraw","partial","none"],"description":"What this block does to earlier text. add: no earlier text stops holding because of it. revise: an earlier block as a whole is taken over by this text (list it in replaces). withdraw: an earlier block as a whole no longer holds and nothing takes its place (list it in replaces). partial: part of an earlier block no longer holds and the rest stands (give overrides). none: the block states no requirement (a preface, a rule line); no object."},"replaces":{"type":"array","items":{"type":"string"},"description":"Earlier units that no longer hold as a whole (revise, withdraw)."},"overrides":{"type":"array","description":"Partial revision: old = earlier units or clauses that no longer hold; by = units of this block that state what holds now. The block keeps its one owner.","properties":{"from":{"type":"string"},"to":{"type":"string"},"kind":{"type":"string","enum":["refers_to","applies_to"]}}}},"edges_remove":{"type":"array","items":{"type":"object","additionalProperties":false,"required":["from","to","kind"],"description":"Only for an object the block's own wording names. refers_to: the block uses what the target block defines; the target's object gets no change. applies_to: the block's requirement also lands on the named object (to = one of its blocks or its id); that object gets a change record. # REQUEST
{"sources":"===== R1 =====
⟦R1.S0#2a4e76a8⟧ ⟦R1.S0.P1#2a4e76a8⟧
‹s1›Build a deterministic data pipeline tool in Go called `dpipe`. ‹s2›‹s2.c1›The tool operates as a CLI that reads structured data from CSV files, ‹s2.c2›applies a chain of transformations, ‹s2.c3›and writes results to output files — with every step producing bit-identical output across repeated runs given the same input and configuration.

⟦R1.S1#645e7240⟧ ## Core behaviors

⟦R1.S2#dda81266⟧ ### Ingestion

⟦R1.S2.P1#70bbdcf1⟧
`dpipe ingest --input <path> --schema <path> --output <path>`

⟦R1.S2.P2#398a6a10⟧
‹s1›- Reads a CSV file at `<path>`. The first row is a header.
‹s2›‹s2.c1›- Validates every row against a JSON schema file. The schema has this structure:
  ```json
  {
    "columns": [
      {"name": "id", "type": "int", "required": true, "unique": true},
      {"name": "value", "type": "float", "required": true, "min": 0, "max": 1000},
      {"name": "label", "type": "string", "required": false, "pattern": "^[A-Z]"},
      {"name": "timestamp", "type": "datetime", "required": true}
    ],
    "primary_key": ["id"]
  }
  ```
  Supported types: `int`, ‹s2.c2›`float`, ‹s2.c3›`string`, ‹s2.c4›`datetime` ‹s2.c5›(RFC 3339 format).

⟦R1.S2.P3#697b6f55⟧
‹s1›‹s1.c1›  Column constraints ‹s1.c2›(all optional):
‹s2›‹s2.c1›  - `unique` ‹s2.c2›(boolean): ‹s2.c3›No two valid rows may have the same value in this column. When a duplicate is encountered ‹s2.c4›(checked in input file order after all other validations pass), ‹s2.c5›the later row is rejected with reason `duplicate value for unique column: <name>`.
‹s3›‹s3.c1›  - `min`, ‹s3.c2›`max` ‹s3.c3›(number): ‹s3.c4›For `int` and `float` columns only. Value must be within `[min, max]` inclusive. Rejected rows get reason `value out of range for column <name>: <value>`.
‹s4›‹s4.c1›  - `pattern` ‹s4.c2›(string): ‹s4.c3›For `string` columns only. Value must match the Go regular expression. Rejected rows get reason `value does not match pattern for column <name>: <value>`.

⟦R1.S2.P4#89c9ed84⟧
‹s1›‹s1.c1›  Validation order for each row: ‹s1.c2›(1) ‹s1.c3›required/type checks, ‹s1.c4›(2) ‹s1.c5›range checks, ‹s1.c6›(3) ‹s1.c7›pattern checks. ‹s2›‹s2.c1›After all rows pass steps 1-3, ‹s2.c2›uniqueness is checked across valid rows in input file order — the first occurrence is kept, ‹s2.c3›subsequent duplicates are rejected.

⟦R1.S2.P5#e86807c6⟧
‹s1.c1›  `primary_key` is always an array of one or more column names ‹s1.c2›(composite key support).

⟦R1.S2.P6#88d8ed51⟧
‹s1›‹s1.c1›- Rows that fail validation are written to `<output>.rejected` ‹s1.c2›(same CSV format, with an appended `rejection_reason` column). ‹s1.c3›Valid rows are written to `<output>` in CSV format.
‹s2›‹s2.c1›- Output rows are sorted by the primary key columns in declaration order: first by the first primary key column, ‹s2.c2›then by the second, ‹s2.c3›etc. Each column is sorted in ascending order using its declared type ‹s2.c4›(numeric sort for int/float, lexicographic for string, chronological for datetime).
‹s3›‹s3.c1›- A SHA-256 checksum of the output file ‹s3.c2›(computed on the raw bytes) ‹s3.c3›is written to `<output>.sha256` as a single hex string followed by a newline.

⟦R1.S3#d66eb59e⟧ ### Transformation

⟦R1.S3.P1#8a0428a9⟧
`dpipe transform --input <path> --recipe <path> --output <path> --seed <uint64>`

⟦R1.S3.P2#5f08913b⟧
‹s1›‹s1.c1›- Reads a CSV file with a header row. In typical usage this will be a previously ingested ‹s1.c2›(valid) ‹s1.c3›CSV file, ‹s1.c4›but any headered CSV input is allowed.
‹s2›‹s2.c1›- Applies transformations defined in a JSON recipe file, ‹s2.c2›in order. Each transformation is an object in an array:
  ```json
  [
    {"op": "filter", "column": "value", "condition": "gt", "threshold": 10.0},
    {"op": "derive", "name": "score", "expression": "value * 2 + 1"},
    {"op": "sample", "fraction": 0.5},
    {"op": "sort", "column": "score", "order": "desc"},
    {"op": "rename", "from": "label", "to": "category"},
    {"op": "drop", "columns": ["timestamp"]},
    {"op": "aggregate", "group_by": ["label"], "aggregations": [
      {"column": "value", "function": "sum", "as": "total_value"},
      {"column": "value", "function": "avg", "as": "avg_value"},
      {"column": "id", "function": "count", "as": "num_items"}
    ]},
    {"op": "join", "right": "other.csv", "on": "id", "type": "left"},
    {"op": "window", "function": "rank", "partition_by": ["label"], "order_by": [{"column": "value", "order": "desc"}], "as": "value_rank"},
    {"op": "pivot", "index": ["id"], "column": "label", "value": "value"},
    {"op": "unpivot", "index": ["id"], "columns": ["q1", "q2", "q3"], "name_to": "quarter", "value_to": "amount"},
    {"op": "fill", "columns": ["value"], "strategy": "forward"}
  ]
  ```
‹s3›- Supported operations:
‹s4›‹s4.c1›  - `filter`: Keep rows where `column` satisfies `condition` against `threshold`. Conditions: `gt`, ‹s4.c2›`gte`, ‹s4.c3›`lt`, ‹s4.c4›`lte`, ‹s4.c5›`eq`, ‹s4.c6›`neq`.
‹s5›  - `derive`: Add a new column computed from an expression over existing numeric columns.

⟦R1.S3.P3#a8cbbd3f⟧
‹s1›‹s1.c1›    **Operator precedence** ‹s1.c2›(lowest to highest):
‹s2›‹s2.c1›    1. `||` ‹s2.c2›(logical OR): ‹s2.c3›returns `1` if either operand is > 0, ‹s2.c4›otherwise `0`
‹s3›‹s3.c1›    2. `&&` ‹s3.c2›(logical AND): ‹s3.c3›returns `1` if both operands are > 0, ‹s3.c4›otherwise `0`
‹s4›‹s4.c1›    3. `==`, `!=` ‹s4.c2›(equality): ‹s4.c3›numeric comparison, ‹s4.c4›returns `1` ‹s4.c5›(true) ‹s4.c6›or `0` ‹s4.c7›(false)
‹s5›‹s5.c1›    4. `>`, `>=`, `<`, `<=` ‹s5.c2›(relational): ‹s5.c3›numeric comparison, ‹s5.c4›returns `1` or `0`
‹s6›‹s6.c1›    5. `+`, `-` ‹s6.c2›(addition, subtraction)
‹s7›‹s7.c1›    6. `*`, `/`, `%` ‹s7.c2›(multiplication, division, modulo)
‹s8›‹s8.c1›    7. Unary `-` ‹s8.c2›(negation)
‹s9›‹s9.c1›    8. Function calls, ‹s9.c2›parentheses, ‹s9.c3›column references, ‹s9.c4›numeric literals

⟦R1.S3.P4#92fb6c93⟧
‹s1›    Division by zero produces `NaN`. ‹s2›Modulo by zero produces `NaN`. ‹s3›‹s3.c1›Any comparison involving `NaN` ‹s3.c2›(on either side) ‹s3.c3›produces `0`.

⟦R1.S3.P5#9f282270⟧
‹s1›‹s1.c1›    The expression evaluator also supports function calls with parenthesized, ‹s1.c2›comma-separated arguments:
‹s2›    - `abs(x)` — absolute value
‹s3›‹s3.c1›    - `sqrt(x)` — square root; ‹s3.c2›returns `NaN` for negative input
‹s4›    - `ceil(x)` — smallest integer >= x
‹s5›    - `floor(x)` — largest integer <= x
‹s6›‹s6.c1›    - `round(x, n)` — round x to n decimal places ‹s6.c2›(n is a non-negative integer; half-values round away from zero)
‹s7›    - `pow(x, y)` — x raised to the power y
‹s8›‹s8.c1›    - `log(x)` — natural logarithm; ‹s8.c2›returns `NaN` for non-positive input
‹s9›    - `min(x, y)` — minimum of two values
‹s10›    - `max(x, y)` — maximum of two values
‹s11›‹s11.c1›    - `if(cond, x, y)` — returns x if cond > 0, ‹s11.c2›otherwise returns y
‹s12›‹s12.c1›    - `clamp(x, lo, hi)` — returns lo if x < lo, ‹s12.c2›hi if x > hi, ‹s12.c3›otherwise x
‹s13›‹s13.c1›    - `coalesce(x, y)` — returns x if x is not NaN, ‹s13.c2›otherwise returns y

⟦R1.S3.P6#b8b7141a⟧
    Functions can be nested: `round(sqrt(abs(value)), 2)`.

⟦R1.S3.P7#0f97dc1b⟧
‹s1.c1›    Comparison and logical operators enable inline conditions without `if`: e.g., ‹s1.c2›`(value > 10 && value < 100) * value` yields `value` when in range, ‹s1.c3›`0` otherwise.

⟦R1.S3.P8#17f7eb48⟧
‹s1›‹s1.c1›    Formatting: derive results are written using the shortest decimal representation that preserves the computed value, ‹s1.c2›without unnecessary trailing zeros or a trailing decimal point ‹s1.c3›(e.g., `11` not `11.0`, `2.5` not `2.50`). ‹s2›`NaN` is written as the literal string `NaN`.

⟦R1.S3.P9#ade451fd⟧
‹s1›‹s1.c1›  - `sample`: Retain the given fraction of rows. The selection must be deterministic given `--seed`. Use the seed to initialize a deterministic PRNG ‹s1.c2›(use Go's `math/rand` with the given seed). ‹s1.c3›Rows are selected by generating a random float for each row in input order; ‹s1.c4›keep the row if the float is < fraction.
‹s2›‹s2.c1›  - `sort`: Sort rows by the given column. `asc` or `desc`. Ties are broken by the original row order ‹s2.c2›(stable sort).
‹s3›  - `rename`: Rename a column.
‹s4›  - `drop`: Remove the listed columns.
‹s5›  - `aggregate`: Group rows by the `group_by` columns and compute aggregations on each group.
    Supported aggregation functions:
‹s6›    - `sum`: sum of numeric values in the column for this group. Empty/non-numeric values are skipped. Result is `0` if no numeric values exist.
‹s7›    - `avg`: arithmetic mean of numeric values. Empty/non-numeric values are skipped. Result is `NaN` if no numeric values exist.
‹s8›    - `count`: number of non-empty values in the specified column for this group.
‹s9›    - `min`: minimum numeric value. Empty/non-numeric values are skipped. Result is `NaN` if no numeric values exist.
‹s10›    - `max`: maximum numeric value. Empty/non-numeric values are skipped. Result is `NaN` if no numeric values exist.

⟦R1.S3.P10#62f372a5⟧
‹s1›‹s1.c1›    Output columns: the group_by columns ‹s1.c2›(in declaration order), ‹s1.c3›followed by the aggregation result columns ‹s1.c4›(in declaration order, using the `as` name). ‹s2›‹s2.c1›Output rows are sorted by the group_by columns in ascending lexicographic order, ‹s2.c2›comparing left to right. ‹s3›‹s3.c1›Numeric aggregation results are formatted without unnecessary trailing zeros ‹s3.c2›(e.g., `10` not `10.0`, `2.5` not `2.50`).

⟦R1.S3.P11#0ec0df15⟧
‹s1›‹s1.c1›    Optional `having` clause: after aggregation results are computed and formatted, ‹s1.c2›filter output rows based on an aggregated column. ‹s2›Example:
‹s3›    ```json
    {"op": "aggregate", "group_by": ["label"], "aggregations": [
      {"column": "value", "function": "sum", "as": "total"}
    ], "having": {"column": "total", "condition": "gt", "threshold": 100}}
    ```

⟦R2.S1#ea12c8ff⟧ ## New command: `profile`

⟦R2.S1.P1#f108f097⟧

⟦R2.S1.P2#8f43e4bd⟧
‹s1.c1›Reads a CSV file ‹s1.c2›(first row is header), ‹s1.c3›infers column types from data, ‹s1.c4›and writes a JSON statistical profile to the output path.

⟦R2.S2#c57b2351⟧ ### Type inference

⟦R2.S2.P1#6104aa8d⟧
‹s1.c1›Since `profile` operates without a schema, ‹s1.c2›column types are inferred from non-empty values:

⟦R2.S2.P2#fd540849⟧
‹s1›‹s1.c1›1. If **all** non-empty values parse as integers ‹s1.c2›(Go's `strconv.ParseInt` with base 10, bit size 64): ‹s1.c3›type is `int`.
‹s2›‹s2.c1›2. Else if all non-empty values parse as floats ‹s2.c2›(Go's `strconv.ParseFloat` with bit size 64): ‹s2.c3›type is `float`.
‹s3›3. Else if all non-empty values parse as RFC 3339 datetimes: type is `datetime`.
‹s4›4. Otherwise: type is `string`.
‹s5›5. A column with zero non-empty values has type `string`.

⟦R2.S2.P3#8dbfa782⟧
‹s1.c1›Note: every valid integer string also parses as a float, ‹s1.c2›so the order matters — try integer first.

⟦R2.S3.P5#391c37c3⟧
‹s1›**`int` and `float` columns** additionally contain:

⟦R2.S3.P6#bfc21664⟧
‹s1›‹s1.c1›**Percentile calculation** ‹s1.c2›(for `median`, `p25`, `p75`): ‹s1.c3›sort the `n` non-empty numeric values in ascending order. ‹s2›‹s2.c1›Compute the index: `idx = p / 100 * (n - 1)` where `p` is the percentile ‹s2.c2›(25, 50, or 75). ‹s3›‹s3.c1›If `idx` is an integer, ‹s3.c2›the result is `values[idx]`. ‹s4›‹s4.c1›Otherwise, ‹s4.c2›interpolate: `lower = floor(idx)`, ‹s4.c3›`upper = ceil(idx)`, ‹s4.c4›`frac = idx - lower`, ‹s4.c5›`result = values[lower] + frac * (values[upper] - values[lower])`.

⟦R2.S3.P7#33abc88d⟧
‹s1.c1›**Additional numeric statistics** ‹s1.c2›(for `int` and `float` columns):

⟦R2.S3.P8#bc2f8ca3⟧
‹s1›‹s1.c1›- `skewness` ‹s1.c2›(number or null): ‹s1.c3›Adjusted Fisher-Pearson standardized moment coefficient.
‹s2›‹s2.c1›  1. Compute sample standard deviation: `s = sqrt(sum((xi - mean)^2) / (n - 1))`. Note: this uses `n - 1` ‹s2.c2›(Bessel's correction), ‹s2.c3›distinct from the population `stddev` field above which uses `n`.
‹s3›  2. Compute: `skewness = (n / ((n - 1) * (n - 2))) * sum(((xi - mean) / s)^3)`
‹s4›  3. Returns `null` if `n < 3` or `s == 0`.

⟦R2.S3.P9#23258bd7⟧
‹s1›‹s1.c1›- `kurtosis` ‹s1.c2›(number or null): ‹s1.c3›Sample excess kurtosis.
‹s2›  1. Using the same sample standard deviation `s` as skewness.
‹s3›  2. Compute: `kurtosis = ((n * (n + 1)) / ((n - 1) * (n - 2) * (n - 3))) * sum(((xi - mean) / s)^4) - (3 * (n - 1)^2) / ((n - 2) * (n - 3))`
‹s4›  3. Returns `null` if `n < 4` or `s == 0`.

⟦R2.S3.P10#afe56155⟧
‹s1.c1›- `mode` ‹s1.c2›(number or null): ‹s1.c3›The most frequently occurring value. If multiple values share the highest frequency, ‹s1.c4›the smallest value wins. ⟦R2.S4#cf67a4d2⟧ ### Correlation matrix

⟦R2.S4.P1#ff89bdd3⟧
‹s1.c1›The profile output additionally contains a top-level `correlations` array: the Pearson correlation coefficient for every pair of numeric columns ‹s1.c2›(those with inferred type `int` or `float`).

⟦R2.S4.P2#a9c6fd9b⟧
‹s1.c1›For each pair of numeric columns ‹s1.c2›(A, B) ‹s1.c3›where A appears before B in the header:

⟦R2.S4.P3#a827daa7⟧
‹s1›1. Collect **paired observations**: rows where both A and B have non-empty values.
‹s2›2. Let `n` be the number of paired observations.
‹s3›‹s3.c1›3. If `n < 2`, ‹s3.c2›correlation is `null`.
‹s4›‹s4.c1›4. Compute paired means: `mean_a = sum(ai) / n`, ‹s4.c2›`mean_b = sum(bi) / n`.
‹s5›5. Compute `numerator = sum((ai - mean_a) * (bi - mean_b))`.
‹s6›6. Compute `denom = sqrt(sum((ai - mean_a)^2) * sum((bi - mean_b)^2))`.
‹s7›‹s7.c1›7. If `denom == 0` ‹s7.c2›(either column has zero variance in the paired set), ‹s7.c3›correlation is `null`.
‹s8›‹s8.c1›8. Otherwise, ‹s8.c2›`correlation = numerator / denom`.

⟦R2.S4.P4#a6bfaf8d⟧
‹s1›Each entry in the `correlations` array is:

‹s1›‹s1.c1›- `column_a`: the name of the first column ‹s1.c2›(earlier in header order).

‹s3›‹s3.c1›- `correlation`: the Pearson coefficient as a JSON number, ‹s3.c2›or `null` if undefined.

⟦R2.S13#2c622e97⟧ ### Fill `linear` strategy

⟦R2.S13.P1#c7f05473⟧
The existing `fill` transform now supports an additional strategy: `"linear"`.

⟦R2.S13.P2#b1266680⟧

⟦R2.S13.P3#b5d0ff18⟧
For each empty cell in the specified columns:

⟦R2.S13.P4#1c9c3dad⟧
‹s1›‹s1.c1›1. Search upward ‹s1.c2›(decreasing row index) ‹s1.c3›for the nearest non-empty cell whose value parses as a float. Call this the **lower anchor** at index `lo` with value `v_lo`.
‹s2›‹s2.c1›2. Search downward ‹s2.c2›(increasing row index) ‹s2.c3›for the nearest non-empty cell whose value parses as a float. Call this the **upper anchor** at index `hi` with value `v_hi`.
‹s3›‹s3.c1›3. If **both** anchors are found, ‹s3.c2›interpolate: `result = v_lo + (v_hi - v_lo) * (i - lo) / (hi - lo)` where `i` is the current row index.
‹s4›‹s4.c1›4. If either anchor is **missing** ‹s4.c2›(no non-empty numeric value exists above or below), ‹s4.c3›the cell remains empty.
‹s5›‹s5.c1›5. Non-empty cells that do not parse as float are skipped during anchor search ‹s5.c2›(treated as if the cell were empty for interpolation purposes, but they are **not** themselves filled).

⟦R2.S16.P4#b4fc0ae2⟧

⟦R2.S16.P6#3520a712⟧

⟦R2.S16.P7#39eb155b⟧
‹s1.c1›- **`iqr`**: Compute Q1, ‹s1.c2›Q3 using the same percentile method as the `profile` command. IQR = Q3 - Q1. A value is an outlier if `value < Q1 - factor * IQR` or `value > Q3 + factor * IQR`. If fewer than 2 numeric values exist, ‹s1.c3›all get `"0"`.

⟦R2.S16.P8#bd240513⟧
‹s1.c1›- **`zscore`**: Compute population mean and population standard deviation ‹s1.c2›(same formulas as profile's `mean` and `stddev`). ‹s1.c3›A value is an outlier if `|value - mean| / stddev > factor`. If stddev is 0, ‹s1.c4›all values get `"0"`.

⟦R2.S16.P9#4ebe98f6⟧
‹s1.c1›- **`mad`**: Compute median of all numeric values. Compute MAD = median of `|xi - median|` for all numeric values. Compute modified Z-score for each value: `modified_z = 0.6745 * (value - median) / MAD`. A value is an outlier if `|modified_z| > factor`. If MAD is 0: values equal to the median get `"0"`, ‹s1.c2›values not equal to the median get `"1"`.

⟦R2.S17.P7#07250743⟧
‹s1›- **`width`**: Equal-width bins.

‹s3›‹s3.c1›  2. Bin index for value `v`: `i = floor((v - min) / w)`, ‹s3.c2›clamped to `[0, bins - 1]`.

⟦R2.S19.P2#4b2a2c56⟧
‹s1.c1›Reads two CSV files and compares them row-by-row using the specified key columns, ‹s1.c2›producing a JSON diff report.

⟦R2.S20#6d602327⟧ ### Comparison logic

⟦R2.S20.P1#4282a676⟧
‹s1›‹s1.c1›1. Read both CSV files ‹s1.c2›(first row is header).
‹s2›‹s2.c1›2. Both files must have identical headers ‹s2.c2›(same column names in the same order). ‹s2.c3›If not, ‹s2.c4›exit with error: `ERROR: schema mismatch: headers differ`.
‹s3›3. The `--key` flag specifies a comma-separated list of column names that form the composite key.
‹s4›‹s4.c1›4. If any key column does not exist in the header, ‹s4.c2›exit with error: `ERROR: invalid key: column <name> not found`.
‹s5›‹s5.c1›5. Build a composite key for each row by joining the values of the key columns with a null byte ‹s5.c2›(`\x00`) ‹s5.c3›separator.
‹s6›6. Classify rows:
‹s7›   - **added**: key exists in right but not in left.
‹s8›   - **removed**: key exists in left but not in right.
‹s9›‹s9.c1›   - **modified**: key exists in both, ‹s9.c2›but at least one non-key column differs.
‹s10›‹s10.c1›   - Rows with matching keys and identical values in all columns are **unchanged** ‹s10.c2›(not included in changes).
‹s11›‹s11.c1›7. If the left file has duplicate keys, ‹s11.c2›only the first occurrence is used. Same for the right file.

⟦R3.S2#c7f49684⟧ ### Fill linear: boundary extrapolation

⟦R3.S2.P1#964da3dd⟧
The `fill` transform with `"strategy": "linear"` now handles boundary cells differently:

⟦R3.S2.P2#19ddcf9d⟧
‹s1›‹s1.c1›- If only a **lower anchor** exists ‹s1.c2›(no float-parseable non-empty cell found below the current empty cell), ‹s1.c3›the empty cell is filled with the lower anchor's value.
‹s2›‹s2.c1›- If only an **upper anchor** exists ‹s2.c2›(no float-parseable non-empty cell found above the current empty cell), ‹s2.c3›the empty cell is filled with the upper anchor's value.
‹s3›‹s3.c1›- If **both** anchors exist, ‹s3.c2›interpolation works as before: `result = v_lo + (v_hi - v_lo) * (i - lo) / (hi - lo)`.
‹s4›‹s4.c1›- If **neither** anchor exists, ‹s4.c2›the cell remains empty.

⟦R3.S2.P3#bb68fa49⟧
‹s1›‹s1.c1›Previously, ‹s1.c2›cells with only one anchor remained empty. ‹s2›This is now corrected to use constant extrapolation from the nearest available anchor.

⟦R3.S3#a99e16ed⟧ ### Normalize zscore: sample standard deviation

⟦R3.S3.P1#87892e24⟧
‹s1.c1›The `normalize` transform with `"method": "zscore"` now uses **sample standard deviation** ‹s1.c2›(Bessel's correction) ‹s1.c3›instead of population standard deviation:

⟦R3.S3.P2#da271c78⟧
`stddev = sqrt(sum((xi - mean)^2) / (n - 1))`

⟦R3.S3.P3#4b6f473a⟧
‹s1›where `n` is the number of valid numeric values. ‹s2›‹s2.c1›If `n < 2`, ‹s2.c2›all output values are `"0"`. ‹s3›‹s3.c1›If sample stddev is 0, ‹s3.c2›all output values are `"0"`.

⟦R3.S3.P4#a9e112f8⟧
‹s1›‹s1.c1›Previously, ‹s1.c2›population standard deviation ‹s1.c3›(`n` denominator) ‹s1.c4›was used. ‹s2›The `profile` command's `stddev` field is unaffected — it continues to use population standard deviation.

⟦R3.S6#35d039ef⟧ ## New command: `drift`

⟦R3.S6.P1#fecda20b⟧
`dpipe drift --baseline <path> --current <path> --output <path> [--threshold <number>]`

⟦R3.S6.P2#6f6003b4⟧
Compares two CSV data files by computing statistical profiles internally and detecting schema and distribution drift between a baseline and a current dataset.

⟦R3.S7#79ae4b72⟧ ### Parameters

⟦R3.S7.P1#a7a7e7b6⟧
‹s1›- `--baseline`: path to the baseline CSV data file.
‹s2›- `--current`: path to the current CSV data file.
‹s3›- `--output`: path for the drift report JSON file.
‹s4›‹s4.c1›- `--threshold` ‹s4.c2›(optional, default `0.1`): ‹s4.c3›numeric threshold for distribution drift metrics.

⟦R3.S8#0028cafa⟧ ### Drift detection

⟦R3.S8.P1#acba491f⟧
‹s1›‹s1.c1›Build a column-level statistical profile for each CSV file internally ‹s1.c2›(using the same type inference rules and numeric statistics as the `profile` command: type inference, count, null_count, unique, and for numeric columns: min, max, mean, population stddev). ‹s2›Then compare the two profiles column by column.

⟦R3.S8.P2#b62d4004⟧
‹s1.c1›**Schema drift** ‹s1.c2›(checked for every column in either profile):

⟦R3.S8.P3#657b454e⟧
‹s1›- `"column_added"`: column exists in current but not in baseline.
‹s2›- `"column_removed"`: column exists in baseline but not in current.
‹s3›- `"type_changed"`: column exists in both profiles but the `type` field differs.

⟦R3.S8.P4#fbdfc36a⟧
‹s1.c1›**Distribution drift** ‹s1.c2›(checked only for columns present in both profiles with the same numeric type — `"int"` or `"float"` — and both having `count > 0`):

⟦R3.S8.P5#58c97df5⟧
‹s1›- `"mean_shift"`: `|current_mean - baseline_mean| / max(baseline_stddev, 1e-10) > threshold`.
‹s2›‹s2.c1›- `"null_rate_change"`: `|current_null_rate - baseline_null_rate| > threshold`, ‹s2.c2›where `null_rate = null_count / row_count`. If `row_count` is 0, ‹s2.c3›null_rate is 0.
‹s3›- `"range_expansion"`: `(current_max - current_min) > (baseline_max - baseline_min) * (1 + threshold)`.
‹s4›‹s4.c1›- `"unique_ratio_change"`: `|current_unique_ratio - baseline_unique_ratio| > threshold`, ‹s4.c2›where `unique_ratio = unique / count`. If `count` is 0, ‹s4.c3›unique_ratio is 0.

For `"type_changed"`, ‹s3.c4›this is the baseline type as a string. ⟦R3.S10#0217e041⟧ ### Ordering

⟦R3.S10.P1#df5e8e69⟧
The `drifts` array is sorted by:

⟦R3.S14#4e861563⟧ ### `resample`

⟦R3.S14.P1#5c95c238⟧
Stratified resampling to balance class distribution.

⟦R3.S14.P2#3684bcdf⟧
```json
{"op": "resample", "column": "label", "strategy": "oversample", "seed": 42}
```

⟦R3.S14.P3#e5c4ac91⟧
‹s1›‹s1.c1›- `column`: the grouping column. Must exist, ‹s1.c2›otherwise: `ERROR: invalid recipe: column <name> not found`.
‹s2›- `strategy`: `"oversample"` or `"undersample"`.
‹s3›‹s3.c1›- `seed` ‹s3.c2›(integer): ‹s3.c3›deterministic random seed for the `undersample` strategy. Ignored by `oversample`.

⟦R3.S14.P4#191283b8⟧
**`oversample`** strategy:

⟦R3.S14.P5#6a715f40⟧
‹s1›‹s1.c1›1. Group rows by the value in `column`. Sort group keys ascending ‹s1.c2›(lexicographic).
‹s2›‹s2.c1›2. Find the maximum group size ‹s2.c2›(`target`).
‹s3›‹s3.c1›3. For each group with fewer than `target` rows, ‹s3.c2›repeat the group's rows cyclically ‹s3.c3›(in their original order within the group) ‹s3.c4›until the group has exactly `target` rows.
‹s4›‹s4.c1›4. Output all rows: groups in sorted key order. Within each group, ‹s4.c2›original rows come first, ‹s4.c3›then oversampled copies.

⟦R3.S14.P6#6a49bf70⟧
**`undersample`** strategy:

⟦R3.S14.P7#bb1b2506⟧
‹s1›‹s1.c1›1. Group rows by the value in `column`. Sort group keys ascending ‹s1.c2›(lexicographic).
‹s2›‹s2.c1›2. Find the minimum group size ‹s2.c2›(`target`).
‹s3›3. For each group with more than `target` rows:
‹s4›   a. Let `groupIndex` be the 0-based index of this group in the sorted group key list.
‹s5›   b. Create an integer array of indices `[0, 1, ..., groupSize-1]`.
‹s6›‹s6.c1›   c. Initialize a deterministic pseudo-random number generator with seed = `seed + groupIndex` ‹s6.c2›(use Go's `math/rand` with `rand.New(rand.NewSource(int64(seed + groupIndex)))`).
‹s7›‹s7.c1›   d. Fisher-Yates shuffle: for `i` from `groupSize - 1` down to `1`, ‹s7.c2›swap `indices[i]` with `indices[rng.Intn(i + 1)]`.
‹s8›‹s8.c1›   e. Take the first `target` elements from the shuffled indices array, ‹s8.c2›sort them ascending.
‹s9›   f. Select the rows at those sorted indices from the group.
‹s10›‹s10.c1›4. For groups with exactly `target` rows, ‹s10.c2›keep all rows.
‹s11›‹s11.c1›5. Output: groups in sorted key order, ‹s11.c2›each group contributing its selected rows in their original relative order.

⟦R5.S1#18045502⟧ ## Behavior Change: verify command checksum algorithm

⟦R5.S1.P1#486a733e⟧
‹s1›The `verify` command previously used SHA256 for computing file checksums. ‹s2›It now uses **BLAKE2b-256** instead.

⟦R5.S1.P2#c7c4509e⟧
‹s1›- The `verify` command still reads the checksum file passed with `--checksum` and compares it against the digest of the file passed with `--file`.
‹s2›‹s2.c1›- Checksums in manifest files must now be BLAKE2b-256 hex digests ‹s2.c2›(64 lowercase hex characters).
‹s3›‹s3.c1›- The `manifest` command must also produce BLAKE2b-256 checksums ‹s3.c2›(not SHA256).
‹s4›- The `.sha256` sidecar files produced during `ingest` and `transform` are **removed** — these commands no longer produce sidecar hash files.
‹s5›‹s5.c1›- If `<output>.sha256` exists from a previous run, ‹s5.c2›`ingest` and `transform` must remove it.
‹s6›‹s6.c1›- BLAKE2b-256 means the standard 256-bit BLAKE2b digest, ‹s6.c2›encoded as 64 lowercase hexadecimal characters.

⟦R5.S1.P3#fd78c019⟧
‹s1›This change affects:
‹s2›1. `manifest` command: produces BLAKE2b-256 checksums instead of SHA256.
‹s3›2. `verify` command: validates against BLAKE2b-256 checksums.
‹s4›3. `ingest` command: no longer writes `.sha256` sidecar files.
‹s5›4. `transform` command: no longer writes `.sha256` sidecar files.

⟦R6.S2#7a74bac4⟧ ### Audit log format

⟦R6.S2.P1#671f5a43⟧
‹s1›The audit log file is a JSON array of entry objects. ‹s2›‹s2.c1›If the file does not exist, ‹s2.c2›create it with a single-element array. ‹s3›‹s3.c1›If the file exists and contains a valid JSON array, ‹s3.c2›append the new entry to the array and write it back. ‹s4›‹s4.c1›If the file exists but is not a valid JSON array, ‹s4.c2›overwrite it with a single-element array containing just the new entry.

⟦R6.S2.P3#6588df30⟧
‹s1›‹s1.c1›- `command` ‹s1.c2›(string): ‹s1.c3›the command name ‹s1.c4›(e.g., `"ingest"`, `"transform"`, `"manifest"`).

‹s5›‹s5.c1›- `success` ‹s5.c2›(bool): ‹s5.c3›true if the command completed without error, ‹s5.c4›false otherwise.

Primary input is: `--input` for transform/profile/validate, ‹s7.c5›`--file` for verify, ‹s7.c6›`--input` for ingest, ‹s7.c7›`--left` for compare, ‹s7.c8›`--baseline` for drift, ‹s7.c9›`--config` for pipeline/lineage. ⟦R6.S5#1b952e0d⟧ ## New transform: `impute`

⟦R6.S5.P1#bc8026a8⟧
‹s1.c1›Fills missing ‹s1.c2›(empty) ‹s1.c3›values in a column using a statistical method computed from non-empty values in that column.

⟦R6.S7.P1#7df98cc1⟧

‹s5›‹s5.c1›   - `"mode"`: most frequent value. If tie, ‹s5.c2›pick the smallest numeric value.

⟦R8.S0#bdada347⟧ ⟦R8.S0.P1#bdada347⟧

⟦R8.S1#8db09131⟧ ## New command: `quality`

⟦R8.S1.P1#09922960⟧
`dpipe quality --input <path> --output <path>`

⟦R8.S1.P2#61c6726a⟧
‹s1.c1›Computes a data quality score for a CSV file based on three dimensions: completeness, ‹s1.c2›consistency, ‹s1.c3›and uniqueness.

⟦R8.S2#ec6dd348⟧ ### Parameters

⟦R8.S2.P1#6a37be32⟧
‹s1›- `--input`: path to the CSV file to analyze.
‹s2›- `--output`: path for the quality report JSON file.

⟦R8.S3#355fa8c6⟧ ### Behavior

⟦R8.S3.P1#3d30586d⟧
‹s1›Read the CSV file. ‹s2›‹s2.c1›For each column, ‹s2.c2›compute:

⟦R8.S3.P2#3436b9d3⟧
‹s1.c1›1. **Completeness**: the fraction of non-empty cells in the column. `completeness = non_empty_count / total_rows`. If total_rows is 0, ‹s1.c2›completeness is 1.0.

⟦R8.S3.P3#2696e220⟧
‹s1›2. **Consistency**: the fraction of non-empty values that match the detected column type. Type detection:
‹s2›‹s2.c1›   - Try parsing all non-empty values as integers ‹s2.c2›(`strconv.ParseInt`, base 10, 64-bit). ‹s2.c3›If all succeed, ‹s2.c4›type is `"int"`.
‹s3›‹s3.c1›   - Otherwise, ‹s3.c2›try parsing all as floats ‹s3.c3›(`strconv.ParseFloat`, 64-bit). ‹s3.c4›If all succeed, ‹s3.c5›type is `"float"`.
‹s4›‹s4.c1›   - Otherwise, ‹s4.c2›type is `"string"` ‹s4.c3›(all values are consistent for string type).
   
⟦R8.S3.P4#c12cf249⟧
‹s1›   `consistency = matching_count / non_empty_count`. ‹s2›‹s2.c1›If non_empty_count is 0, ‹s2.c2›consistency is 1.0.
   
⟦R8.S3.P5#42d0cfee⟧
‹s1›‹s1.c1›   For `"string"` type, ‹s1.c2›consistency is always 1.0. ‹s2›‹s2.c1›For `"int"` and `"float"` types, ‹s2.c2›consistency is the fraction of non-empty values that parse successfully as that type. ‹s3›‹s3.c1›Since type detection already ensures all values parse, ‹s3.c2›consistency for detected int/float is also 1.0. ‹s4›‹s4.c1›However, ‹s4.c2›if the column has mixed types ‹s4.c3›(some int, some float-only like "1.5"), ‹s4.c4›the detected type would be float, ‹s4.c5›and consistency would reflect how many parse as float.

⟦R8.S3.P6#95525831⟧
‹s1.c1›3. **Uniqueness**: the ratio of unique non-empty values to total non-empty values. `uniqueness = unique_count / non_empty_count`. If non_empty_count is 0, ‹s1.c2›uniqueness is 1.0.

⟦R8.S4#629c3df0⟧ ### Per-column output

⟦R8.S4.P1#6eee852a⟧
‹s1›‹s1.c1›For each column, ‹s1.c2›output an object with:
‹s2›‹s2.c1›- `name` ‹s2.c2›(string): ‹s2.c3›column name.
‹s3›‹s3.c1›- `completeness` ‹s3.c2›(float): ‹s3.c3›completeness score.
‹s4›‹s4.c1›- `consistency` ‹s4.c2›(float): ‹s4.c3›consistency score.
‹s5›‹s5.c1›- `uniqueness` ‹s5.c2›(float): ‹s5.c3›uniqueness score.
‹s6›‹s6.c1›- `quality_score` ‹s6.c2›(float): ‹s6.c3›average of completeness, ‹s6.c4›consistency, ‹s6.c5›and uniqueness.
‹s7›‹s7.c1›- `detected_type` ‹s7.c2›(string): ‹s7.c3›`"int"`, ‹s7.c4›`"float"`, ‹s7.c5›or `"string"`.

⟦R8.S5#61cd82fb⟧ ### Overall scores

⟦R8.S5.P1#e76caacc⟧
‹s1›Compute overall scores as the average across all columns:
‹s2›- `overall_completeness`: average of all columns' completeness.
‹s3›- `overall_consistency`: average of all columns' consistency.
‹s4›- `overall_uniqueness`: average of all columns' uniqueness.
‹s5›- `overall_quality_score`: average of all columns' quality_score.

    {

‹s4›‹s4.c1›  - `"partial"`: keep first 2 characters and last 2 characters, ‹s4.c2›replace middle with `***`. If value has 4 or fewer characters, ‹s4.c3›replace with `"****"`.
‹s5›‹s5.c1›  - `"hash"`: SHA256 hex digest of the value, ‹s5.c2›first 8 characters ‹s5.c3›(lowercase).
‹s6›‹s6.c1›- `as`: name of the new column ‹s6.c2›(appended after existing columns).

# SYSTEM
You write acceptance checks for a command-line program from its requirements. `sources` holds every round so far, annotated with block ids; the original text is the only authority and newer text overrides older text.
Write checks for the objects in `scope` (they changed this round), and to replace the checks in `stale` (whose source, a block they refer to, or a convention they use changed); for no other object. A check runs the program once: `input.files` are written into an empty directory, the program is called with `input.args`, and each assertion reads one fact of the result. Command names, options and JSON keys must be those the requirements' code fragments show.
Every expected value needs a source: verbatim when the requirement states it (quote the block's text exactly), derived when you computed it from the input; for derived values also write `reference_script`, an independent computation from the input files that prints {assertion id: value}. Only values on which both agree are kept. Never compute a digest, hash or checksum yourself: an expected one is source computed, and one an input file needs is written as {{computed:NAME}} in the file, with the reference script printing NAME's value; the code fills it in before the program runs.
Keep convention facts (a shared error format, an output-formatting rule) in their own assertions with role convention, and list those conventions in `uses`; business facts are the object's own behaviour.
Every check states its expected exit code. Prefer checks whose expected output depends on the input data; a check of the exit code alone shows little. `checks` lists the library's checks for these objects and `stale` those whose source text changed this round: derive their replacements where the text still says something checkable. You may propose retiring a check whose expectation rests on replaced text; the code verifies the proposal.
Answer as a patch on `previous_draft` (empty on the first call). When `issues` is not empty, fix exactly those problems and leave the rest as it is.

# REQUEST
{"sources":"===== R1 =====
⟦R1.S0#2a4e76a8⟧ ⟦R1.S0.P1#2a4e76a8⟧
‹s1›Build a deterministic data pipeline tool in Go called `dpipe`. ‹s2›‹s2.c1›The tool operates as a CLI that reads structured data from CSV files, ‹s2.c2›applies a chain of transformations, ‹s2.c3›and writes results to output files — with every step producing bit-identical output across repeated runs given the same input and configuration.

⟦R1.S1#645e7240⟧ ## Core behaviors

⟦R1.S2#dda81266⟧ ### Ingestion

⟦R1.S2.P1#70bbdcf1⟧
`dpipe ingest --input <path> --schema <path> --output <path>`

⟦R1.S2.P2#398a6a10⟧
‹s1›- Reads a CSV file at `<path>`. The first row is a header.
‹s2›‹s2.c1›- Validates every row against a JSON schema file. The schema has this structure:
  ```json
  {
    "columns": [
      {"name": "id", "type": "int", "required": true, "unique": true},
      {"name": "value", "type": "float", "required": true, "min": 0, "max": 1000},
      {"name": "label", "type": "string", "required": false, "pattern": "^[A-Z]"},
      {"name": "timestamp", "type": "datetime", "required": true}
    ],
    "primary_key": ["id"]
  }
  ```
  Supported types: `int`, ‹s2.c2›`float`, ‹s2.c3›`string`, ‹s2.c4›`datetime` ‹s2.c5›(RFC 3339 format).

⟦R1.S2.P3#697b6f55⟧
‹s1›‹s1.c1›  Column constraints ‹s1.c2›(all optional):
‹s2›‹s2.c1›  - `unique` ‹s2.c2›(boolean): ‹s2.c3›No two valid rows may have the same value in this column. When a duplicate is encountered ‹s2.c4›(checked in input file order after all other validations pass), ‹s2.c5›the later row is rejected with reason `duplicate value for unique column: <name>`.
‹s3›‹s3.c1›  - `min`, ‹s3.c2›`max` ‹s3.c3›(number): ‹s3.c4›For `int` and `float` columns only. Value must be within `[min, max]` inclusive. Rejected rows get reason `value out of range for column <name>: <value>`.
‹s4›‹s4.c1›  - `pattern` ‹s4.c2›(string): ‹s4.c3›For `string` columns only. Value must match the Go regular expression. Rejected rows get reason `value does not match pattern for column <name>: <value>`.

⟦R1.S2.P4#89c9ed84⟧
‹s1›‹s1.c1›  Validation order for each row: ‹s1.c2›(1) ‹s1.c3›required/type checks, ‹s1.c4›(2) ‹s1.c5›range checks, ‹s1.c6›(3) ‹s1.c7›pattern checks. ‹s2›‹s2.c1›After all rows pass steps 1-3, ‹s2.c2›uniqueness is checked across valid rows in input file order — the first occurrence is kept, ‹s2.c3›subsequent duplicates are rejected.

⟦R1.S2.P5#e86807c6⟧
‹s1.c1›  `primary_key` is always an array of one or more column names ‹s1.c2›(composite key support).

⟦R1.S2.P6#88d8ed51⟧
‹s1›‹s1.c1›- Rows that fail validation are written to `<output>.rejected` ‹s1.c2›(same CSV format, with an appended `rejection_reason` column). ‹s1.c3›Valid rows are written to `<output>` in CSV format.
‹s2›‹s2.c1›- Output rows are sorted by the primary key columns in declaration order: first by the first primary key column, ‹s2.c2›then by the second, ‹s2.c3›etc. Each column is sorted in ascending order using its declared type ‹s2.c4›(numeric sort for int/float, lexicographic for string, chronological for datetime).
‹s3›‹s3.c1›- A SHA-256 checksum of the output file ‹s3.c2›(computed on the raw bytes) ‹s3.c3›is written to `<output>.sha256` as a single hex string followed by a newline.

⟦R1.S3#d66eb59e⟧ ### Transformation

⟦R1.S3.P1#8a0428a9⟧
`dpipe transform --input <path> --recipe <path> --output <path> --seed <uint64>`

⟦R1.S3.P2#5f08913b⟧
‹s1›‹s1.c1›- Reads a CSV file with a header row. In typical usage this will be a previously ingested ‹s1.c2›(valid) ‹s1.c3›CSV file, ‹s1.c4›but any headered CSV input is allowed.
‹s2›‹s2.c1›- Applies transformations defined in a JSON recipe file, ‹s2.c2›in order. Each transformation is an object in an array:
  ```json
  [
    {"op": "filter", "column": "value", "condition": "gt", "threshold": 10.0},
    {"op": "derive", "name": "score", "expression": "value * 2 + 1"},
    {"op": "sample", "fraction": 0.5},
    {"op": "sort", "column": "score", "order": "desc"},
    {"op": "rename", "from": "label", "to": "category"},
    {"op": "drop", "columns": ["timestamp"]},
    {"op": "aggregate", "group_by": ["label"], "aggregations": [
      {"column": "value", "function": "sum", "as": "total_value"},
      {"column": "value", "function": "avg", "as": "avg_value"},
      {"column": "id", "function": "count", "as": "num_items"}
    ]},
    {"op": "join", "right": "other.csv", "on": "id", "type": "left"},
    {"op": "window", "function": "rank", "partition_by": ["label"], "order_by": [{"column": "value", "order": "desc"}], "as": "value_rank"},
    {"op": "pivot", "index": ["id"], "column": "label", "value": "value"},
    {"op": "unpivot", "index": ["id"], "columns": ["q1", "q2", "q3"], "name_to": "quarter", "value_to": "amount"},
    {"op": "fill", "columns": ["value"], "strategy": "forward"}
  ]
  ```
‹s3›- Supported operations:
‹s4›‹s4.c1›  - `filter`: Keep rows where `column` satisfies `condition` against `threshold`. Conditions: `gt`, ‹s4.c2›`gte`, ‹s4.c3›`lt`, ‹s4.c4›`lte`, ‹s4.c5›`eq`, ‹s4.c6›`neq`.
‹s5›  - `derive`: Add a new column computed from an expression over existing numeric columns.

⟦R1.S3.P3#a8cbbd3f⟧
‹s1›‹s1.c1›    **Operator precedence** ‹s1.c2›(lowest to highest):
‹s2›‹s2.c1›    1. `||` ‹s2.c2›(logical OR): ‹s2.c3›returns `1` if either operand is > 0, ‹s2.c4›otherwise `0`
‹s3›‹s3.c1›    2. `&&` ‹s3.c2›(logical AND): ‹s3.c3›returns `1` if both operands are > 0, ‹s3.c4›otherwise `0`
‹s4›‹s4.c1›    3. `==`, `!=` ‹s4.c2›(equality): ‹s4.c3›numeric comparison, ‹s4.c4›returns `1` ‹s4.c5›(true) ‹s4.c6›or `0` ‹s4.c7›(false)
‹s5›‹s5.c1›    4. `>`, `>=`, `<`, `<=` ‹s5.c2›(relational): ‹s5.c3›numeric comparison, ‹s5.c4›returns `1` or `0`
‹s6›‹s6.c1›    5. `+`, `-` ‹s6.c2›(addition, subtraction)
‹s7›‹s7.c1›    6. `*`, `/`, `%` ‹s7.c2›(multiplication, division, modulo)
‹s8›‹s8.c1›    7. Unary `-` ‹s8.c2›(negation)
‹s9›‹s9.c1›    8. Function calls, ‹s9.c2›parentheses, ‹s9.c3›column references, ‹s9.c4›numeric literals

⟦R1.S3.P4#92fb6c93⟧
‹s1›    Division by zero produces `NaN`. ‹s2›Modulo by zero produces `NaN`. ‹s3›‹s3.c1›Any comparison involving `NaN` ‹s3.c2›(on either side) ‹s3.c3›produces `0`.

⟦R1.S3.P5#9f282270⟧
‹s1›‹s1.c1›    The expression evaluator also supports function calls with parenthesized, ‹s1.c2›comma-separated arguments:
‹s2›    - `abs(x)` — absolute value
‹s3›‹s3.c1›    - `sqrt(x)` — square root; ‹s3.c2›returns `NaN` for negative input
‹s4›    - `ceil(x)` — smallest integer >= x
‹s5›    - `floor(x)` — largest integer <= x
‹s6›‹s6.c1›    - `round(x, n)` — round x to n decimal places ‹s6.c2›(n is a non-negative integer; half-values round away from zero)
‹s7›    - `pow(x, y)` — x raised to the power y
‹s8›‹s8.c1›    - `log(x)` — natural logarithm; ‹s8.c2›returns `NaN` for non-positive input
‹s9›    - `min(x, y)` — minimum of two values
‹s10›    - `max(x, y)` — maximum of two values
‹s11›‹s11.c1›    - `if(cond, x, y)` — returns x if cond > 0, ‹s11.c2›otherwise returns y
‹s12›‹s12.c1›    - `clamp(x, lo, hi)` — returns lo if x < lo, ‹s12.c2›hi if x > hi, ‹s12.c3›otherwise x
‹s13›‹s13.c1›    - `coalesce(x, y)` — returns x if x is not NaN, ‹s13.c2›otherwise returns y

⟦R1.S3.P6#b8b7141a⟧
    Functions can be nested: `round(sqrt(abs(value)), 2)`.

⟦R1.S3.P7#0f97dc1b⟧
‹s1.c1›    Comparison and logical operators enable inline conditions without `if`: e.g., ‹s1.c2›`(value > 10 && value < 100) * value` yields `value` when in range, ‹s1.c3›`0` otherwise.

⟦R1.S3.P8#17f7eb48⟧
‹s1›‹s1.c1›    Formatting: derive results are written using the shortest decimal representation that preserves the computed value, ‹s1.c2›without unnecessary trailing zeros or a trailing decimal point ‹s1.c3›(e.g., `11` not `11.0`, `2.5` not `2.50`). ‹s2›`NaN` is written as the literal string `NaN`.

⟦R1.S3.P9#ade451fd⟧
‹s1›‹s1.c1›  - `sample`: Retain the given fraction of rows. The selection must be deterministic given `--seed`. Use the seed to initialize a deterministic PRNG ‹s1.c2›(use Go's `math/rand` with the given seed). ‹s1.c3›Rows are selected by generating a random float for each row in input order; ‹s1.c4›keep the row if the float is < fraction.
‹s2›‹s2.c1›  - `sort`: Sort rows by the given column. `asc` or `desc`. Ties are broken by the original row order ‹s2.c2›(stable sort).
‹s3›  - `rename`: Rename a column.
‹s4›  - `drop`: Remove the listed columns.
‹s5›  - `aggregate`: Group rows by the `group_by` columns and compute aggregations on each group.
    Supported aggregation functions:
‹s6›    - `sum`: sum of numeric values in the column for this group. Empty/non-numeric values are skipped. Result is `0` if no numeric values exist.
‹s7›    - `avg`: arithmetic mean of numeric values. Empty/non-numeric values are skipped. Result is `NaN` if no numeric values exist.
‹s8›    - `count`: number of non-empty values in the specified column for this group.
‹s9›    - `min`: minimum numeric value. Empty/non-numeric values are skipped. Result is `NaN` if no numeric values exist.
‹s10›    - `max`: maximum numeric value. Empty/non-numeric values are skipped. Result is `NaN` if no numeric values exist.

⟦R1.S3.P10#62f372a5⟧
‹s1›‹s1.c1›    Output columns: the group_by columns ‹s1.c2›(in declaration order), ‹s1.c3›followed by the aggregation result columns ‹s1.c4›(in declaration order, using the `as` name). ‹s2›‹s2.c1›Output rows are sorted by the group_by columns in ascending lexicographic order, ‹s2.c2›comparing left to right. ‹s3›‹s3.c1›Numeric aggregation results are formatted without unnecessary trailing zeros ‹s3.c2›(e.g., `10` not `10.0`, `2.5` not `2.50`).

⟦R1.S3.P11#0ec0df15⟧
‹s1›‹s1.c1›    Optional `having` clause: after aggregation results are computed and formatted, ‹s1.c2›filter output rows based on an aggregated column. ‹s2›Example:
‹s3›    ```json
    {"op": "aggregate", "group_by": ["label"], "aggregations": [
      {"column": "value", "function": "sum", "as": "total"}
    ], "having": {"column": "total", "condition": "gt", "threshold": 100}}
    ```
‹s4›‹s4.c1›    The `having` object uses the same condition operators as `filter` ‹s4.c2›(`gt`, `gte`, `lt`, `lte`, `eq`, `neq`). ‹s5›The `column` must reference one of the `as` names from the aggregations. ‹s6›‹s6.c1›The threshold comparison is numeric ‹s6.c2›(the aggregated result string is parsed as a float). ‹s7›Groups whose aggregated value does not satisfy the condition are excluded from output. ‹s8›‹s8.c1›The `having` clause is applied after sorting — it only removes rows, ‹s8.c2›it does not change the relative order of remaining rows.

⟦R1.S3.P12#f683eb75⟧
‹s1›  - `join`: Join current dataset with another CSV file.
‹s2›    - `right`: path to the other CSV file
‹s3›‹s3.c1›    - `on`: column name that must exist in both datasets ‹s3.c2›(the join key)
‹s4›    - `type`: `"inner"` or `"left"`
‹s5›      - `inner`: output only rows where the join key value exists in both datasets
‹s6›‹s6.c1›      - `left`: output all rows from the current ‹s6.c2›(left) ‹s6.c3›dataset; ‹s6.c4›for rows where the join key has no match in the right dataset, ‹s6.c5›all right-side columns are filled with empty strings
‹s7›‹s7.c1›    - Output columns: all columns from the left dataset, ‹s7.c2›followed by all columns from the right dataset *except* the join key column ‹s7.c3›(to avoid duplication).
‹s8›‹s8.c1›    - If multiple rows in the right dataset share the same join key, ‹s8.c2›only the first one ‹s8.c3›(by file order) ‹s8.c4›is used.
‹s9›‹s9.c1›    - Output rows preserve the order of the left ‹s9.c2›(current) ‹s9.c3›dataset.
‹s10›‹s10.c1›    - If the join key column does not exist in either dataset, ‹s10.c2›exit with error: `ERROR: invalid recipe: join key <name> not found in <left|right> dataset`.

⟦R1.S3.P13#81ee37a3⟧
‹s1›  - `window`: Add a new column computed by a window function over partitions of the data.
‹s2›‹s2.c1›    - `partition_by` ‹s2.c2›(optional): ‹s2.c3›array of column names to partition by. If omitted or empty, ‹s2.c4›all rows are in one partition.
‹s3›‹s3.c1›    - `order_by`: array of ordering specifications, ‹s3.c2›each an object with `"column"` ‹s3.c3›(string) ‹s3.c4›and `"order"` ‹s3.c5›(`"asc"` or `"desc"`). ‹s3.c6›Rows within each partition are ordered by these columns ‹s3.c7›(first column is primary, etc.). ‹s3.c8›Ties in all order_by columns are broken by input row order.
‹s4›    - `as`: name of the new column to create.

⟦R1.S3.P14#1b600a68⟧
‹s1›‹s1.c1›    Supported window functions ‹s1.c2›(specified in the `"function"` field):
‹s2›‹s2.c1›    - `rank`: 1-based rank within the partition. Rows with equal values in all `order_by` columns receive the same rank. The next rank after a group of ties skips ahead by the group size ‹s2.c2›(e.g., two rows tied at rank 1 → next rank is 3).
‹s3›‹s3.c1›    - `dense_rank`: Like `rank` but without gaps ‹s3.c2›(e.g., two rows tied at rank 1 → next rank is 2).
‹s4›    - `row_number`: Unique sequential number starting from 1 within the partition. Ties are broken by input row order.
‹s5›‹s5.c1›    - `lag`: Value of a source column from a preceding row in partition order. Additional operation fields: `"source_column"` ‹s5.c2›(string), ‹s5.c3›`"offset"` ‹s5.c4›(positive integer, number of rows back), ‹s5.c5›`"default"` ‹s5.c6›(string, value to use when no preceding row exists at that offset). ‹s5.c7›Example:
      ```json
      {"op": "window", "function": "lag", "source_column": "value", "offset": 1, "default": "0", "partition_by": ["cat"], "order_by": [{"column": "id", "order": "asc"}], "as": "prev_value"}
      ```
‹s6›‹s6.c1›    - `lead`: Like `lag` but looks forward ‹s6.c2›(rows ahead in partition order). ‹s6.c3›Same additional fields as `lag`.
‹s7›‹s7.c1›    - `running_sum`: Cumulative sum of a source column's values up to and including the current row within the partition ‹s7.c2›(in partition order). ‹s7.c3›Additional field: `"source_column"`. Non-numeric values are treated as 0. Example:
      ```json
      {"op": "window", "function": "running_sum", "source_column": "value", "partition_by": ["cat"], "order_by": [{"column": "id", "order": "asc"}], "as": "cum_value"}
      ```
‹s8›‹s8.c1›    - `running_avg`: Cumulative average of a source column's numeric values up to and including the current row. Additional field: `"source_column"`. Non-numeric values are skipped from both numerator and denominator. If no numeric values exist up to the current row, ‹s8.c2›the result is `NaN`.
‹s9›‹s9.c1›    - `ntile`: Divide the partition into `n` roughly equal groups numbered 1 through `n`. Additional field: `"n"` ‹s9.c2›(positive integer). ‹s9.c3›If the partition has `k` rows, ‹s9.c4›the first `k mod n` groups have `ceil(k/n)` rows each, ‹s9.c5›and the remaining groups have `floor(k/n)` rows each. Example:
      ```json
      {"op": "window", "function": "ntile", "n": 4, "partition_by": [], "order_by": [{"column": "id", "order": "asc"}], "as": "quartile"}
      ```

⟦R1.S3.P15#0b65801e⟧
‹s1›‹s1.c1›    Output: all original columns in their original order, ‹s1.c2›plus the new column appended. ‹s2›‹s2.c1›Output rows preserve the original input row order ‹s2.c2›(not the partition order).

⟦R1.S3.P16#5b56d2d3⟧
‹s1›‹s1.c1›    Formatting: `rank`, ‹s1.c2›`dense_rank`, ‹s1.c3›`row_number`, ‹s1.c4›and `ntile` results are formatted as integers ‹s1.c5›(no decimal point). ‹s2›‹s2.c1›`running_sum`, ‹s2.c2›`running_avg`, ‹s2.c3›`lag`, ‹s2.c4›and `lead` results are formatted without unnecessary trailing zeros.

⟦R1.S3.P17#577f7453⟧
‹s1.c1›    If any referenced column ‹s1.c2›(in `partition_by`, `order_by`, or `source_column`) ‹s1.c3›does not exist, ‹s1.c4›exit with error: `ERROR: invalid recipe: column <name> not found`.

⟦R1.S3.P18#077cce58⟧
‹s1›  - `pivot`: Reshape data from long format to wide format.
‹s2›‹s2.c1›    - `index`: array of column names that identify each output row ‹s2.c2›(the row keys).
‹s3›    - `column`: the column whose unique values become new column headers.
‹s4›    - `value`: the column whose values fill the cells.

⟦R1.S3.P19#c21ad861⟧
‹s1›    Behavior:

⟦R2.S0#aa425d1f⟧ ⟦R2.S0.P1#aa425d1f⟧
Add the following capabilities to `dpipe`.

⟦R2.S1#ea12c8ff⟧ ## New command: `profile`

⟦R2.S1.P1#f108f097⟧
`dpipe profile --input <path> --output <path>`

⟦R2.S1.P2#8f43e4bd⟧
‹s1.c1›Reads a CSV file ‹s1.c2›(first row is header), ‹s1.c3›infers column types from data, ‹s1.c4›and writes a JSON statistical profile to the output path.

⟦R2.S2#c57b2351⟧ ### Type inference

⟦R2.S2.P1#6104aa8d⟧
‹s1.c1›Since `profile` operates without a schema, ‹s1.c2›column types are inferred from non-empty values:

⟦R2.S2.P2#fd540849⟧
‹s1›‹s1.c1›1. If **all** non-empty values parse as integers ‹s1.c2›(Go's `strconv.ParseInt` with base 10, bit size 64): ‹s1.c3›type is `int`.
‹s2›‹s2.c1›2. Else if all non-empty values parse as floats ‹s2.c2›(Go's `strconv.ParseFloat` with bit size 64): ‹s2.c3›type is `float`.
‹s3›3. Else if all non-empty values parse as RFC 3339 datetimes: type is `datetime`.
‹s4›4. Otherwise: type is `string`.
‹s5›5. A column with zero non-empty values has type `string`.

⟦R2.S2.P3#8dbfa782⟧
‹s1.c1›Note: every valid integer string also parses as a float, ‹s1.c2›so the order matters — try integer first.

⟦R2.S3#e3530a08⟧ ### Output format

⟦R2.S3.P1#da9cd26d⟧
```json
{
  "row_count": 100,
  "columns": [
    {
      "name": "id",
      "type": "int",
      "count": 100,
      "null_count": 0,
      "unique": 100,
      "min": 1,
      "max": 100,
      "mean": 50.5,
      "stddev": 28.86607004772212,
      "median": 50.5,
      "p25": 25.75,
      "p75": 75.25
    }
  ],
  "correlations": [
    {"column_a": "id", "column_b": "score", "correlation": 0.95},
    {"column_a": "id", "column_b": "value", "correlation": null}
  ]
}
```

⟦R2.S3.P2#a86e165f⟧
‹s1.c1›The `columns` array contains one object per CSV column, ‹s1.c2›in column declaration order ‹s1.c3›(left to right in the header).

⟦R2.S3.P3#9df43b0c⟧
‹s1›Each column object always contains:
‹s2›‹s2.c1›- `name` ‹s2.c2›(string): ‹s2.c3›the column header name.
‹s3›‹s3.c1›- `type` ‹s3.c2›(string): ‹s3.c3›the inferred type ‹s3.c4›(`"int"`, `"float"`, `"string"`, or `"datetime"`).
‹s4›‹s4.c1›- `count` ‹s4.c2›(integer): ‹s4.c3›number of non-empty values.
‹s5›‹s5.c1›- `null_count` ‹s5.c2›(integer): ‹s5.c3›number of empty values ‹s5.c4›(`row_count - count`).
‹s6›‹s6.c1›- `unique` ‹s6.c2›(integer): ‹s6.c3›number of distinct non-empty values.

⟦R2.S3.P4#cd720aaf⟧
Additional fields depend on the inferred type:

⟦R2.S3.P5#391c37c3⟧
‹s1›**`int` and `float` columns** additionally contain:
‹s2›‹s2.c1›- `min`: minimum value. JSON integer for `int` columns, ‹s2.c2›JSON number for `float` columns.
‹s3›- `max`: maximum value. Same formatting as `min`.
‹s4›‹s4.c1›- `mean` ‹s4.c2›(number): ‹s4.c3›arithmetic mean.
‹s5›‹s5.c1›- `stddev` ‹s5.c2›(number): ‹s5.c3›population standard deviation = `sqrt(sum((xi - mean)^2) / n)`. For a single value, ‹s5.c4›`stddev` is `0`.
‹s6›‹s6.c1›- `median` ‹s6.c2›(number): ‹s6.c3›50th percentile.
‹s7›‹s7.c1›- `p25` ‹s7.c2›(number): ‹s7.c3›25th percentile.
‹s8›‹s8.c1›- `p75` ‹s8.c2›(number): ‹s8.c3›75th percentile.

⟦R2.S3.P6#bfc21664⟧
‹s1›‹s1.c1›**Percentile calculation** ‹s1.c2›(for `median`, `p25`, `p75`): ‹s1.c3›sort the `n` non-empty numeric values in ascending order. ‹s2›‹s2.c1›Compute the index: `idx = p / 100 * (n - 1)` where `p` is the percentile ‹s2.c2›(25, 50, or 75). ‹s3›‹s3.c1›If `idx` is an integer, ‹s3.c2›the result is `values[idx]`. ‹s4›‹s4.c1›Otherwise, ‹s4.c2›interpolate: `lower = floor(idx)`, ‹s4.c3›`upper = ceil(idx)`, ‹s4.c4›`frac = idx - lower`, ‹s4.c5›`result = values[lower] + frac * (values[upper] - values[lower])`.

⟦R2.S3.P7#33abc88d⟧
‹s1.c1›**Additional numeric statistics** ‹s1.c2›(for `int` and `float` columns):

⟦R2.S3.P8#bc2f8ca3⟧
‹s1›‹s1.c1›- `skewness` ‹s1.c2›(number or null): ‹s1.c3›Adjusted Fisher-Pearson standardized moment coefficient.
‹s2›‹s2.c1›  1. Compute sample standard deviation: `s = sqrt(sum((xi - mean)^2) / (n - 1))`. Note: this uses `n - 1` ‹s2.c2›(Bessel's correction), ‹s2.c3›distinct from the population `stddev` field above which uses `n`.
‹s3›  2. Compute: `skewness = (n / ((n - 1) * (n - 2))) * sum(((xi - mean) / s)^3)`
‹s4›  3. Returns `null` if `n < 3` or `s == 0`.

⟦R2.S3.P9#23258bd7⟧
‹s1›‹s1.c1›- `kurtosis` ‹s1.c2›(number or null): ‹s1.c3›Sample excess kurtosis.
‹s2›  1. Using the same sample standard deviation `s` as skewness.
‹s3›  2. Compute: `kurtosis = ((n * (n + 1)) / ((n - 1) * (n - 2) * (n - 3))) * sum(((xi - mean) / s)^4) - (3 * (n - 1)^2) / ((n - 2) * (n - 3))`
‹s4›  3. Returns `null` if `n < 4` or `s == 0`.

⟦R2.S3.P10#afe56155⟧
‹s1.c1›- `mode` ‹s1.c2›(number or null): ‹s1.c3›The most frequently occurring value. If multiple values share the highest frequency, ‹s1.c4›the smallest value wins. Returns `null` if count is `0` or if every non-empty value appears exactly once. For `int` columns, ‹s1.c5›`mode` is a JSON integer; ‹s1.c6›for `float` columns, ‹s1.c7›a JSON number.

⟦R2.S3.P11#ced0bd3a⟧
‹s1›‹s1.c1›- `histogram` ‹s1.c2›(array of objects): ‹s1.c3›10 equal-width bins spanning the range of values.
‹s2›  - Compute `width = (max - min) / 10`.
‹s3›‹s3.c1›  - Bin `i` ‹s3.c2›(0-indexed, 0 to 9): ‹s3.c3›`low = min + i * width`, ‹s3.c4›`high = min + (i + 1) * width`.
‹s4›‹s4.c1›  - Assignment: a value `v` goes into bin `floor((v - min) / width)`, ‹s4.c2›clamped to `[0, 9]`. This means bins 0–8 are `[low, high)` ‹s4.c3›(left-inclusive, right-exclusive) ‹s4.c4›and bin 9 is `[low, max]` ‹s4.c5›(inclusive on both ends).
‹s5›  - Each object: `{"low": <number>, "high": <number>, "count": <integer>}`. `low` and `high` use the same JSON number formatting as other profile statistics.
‹s6›‹s6.c1›  - If all values are identical ‹s6.c2›(`max == min`): ‹s6.c3›return a single-element array `[{"low": <value>, "high": <value>, "count": n}]`.
‹s7›  - Empty array `[]` if count is `0`.

⟦R2.S3.P12#6d1e8a8e⟧
‹s1›**`string` columns** additionally contain:
‹s2›‹s2.c1›- `min_length` ‹s2.c2›(integer): ‹s2.c3›minimum byte length among non-empty values. `0` if count is `0`.
‹s3›‹s3.c1›- `max_length` ‹s3.c2›(integer): ‹s3.c3›maximum byte length among non-empty values. `0` if count is `0`.
‹s4›‹s4.c1›- `most_common` ‹s4.c2›(array): ‹s4.c3›top 5 most frequent non-empty values, ‹s4.c4›sorted by count descending; ‹s4.c5›ties broken by value ascending ‹s4.c6›(lexicographic). ‹s4.c7›Each entry: `{"value": "...", "count": N}`. If fewer than 5 unique values exist, ‹s4.c8›include all. Empty array if count is `0`.
‹s5›‹s5.c1›- `avg_length` ‹s5.c2›(number): ‹s5.c3›average byte length among non-empty values. `0` if count is `0`.

⟦R2.S3.P13#ee55b0e3⟧
‹s1›**`datetime` columns** additionally contain:
‹s2›‹s2.c1›- `earliest` ‹s2.c2›(string): ‹s2.c3›the earliest datetime value formatted as RFC 3339.
‹s3›‹s3.c1›- `latest` ‹s3.c2›(string): ‹s3.c3›the latest datetime value formatted as RFC 3339.

⟦R2.S4#cf67a4d2⟧ ### Correlation matrix

⟦R2.S4.P1#ff89bdd3⟧
‹s1.c1›The profile output additionally contains a top-level `correlations` array: the Pearson correlation coefficient for every pair of numeric columns ‹s1.c2›(those with inferred type `int` or `float`).

⟦R2.S4.P2#a9c6fd9b⟧
‹s1.c1›For each pair of numeric columns ‹s1.c2›(A, B) ‹s1.c3›where A appears before B in the header:

⟦R2.S4.P3#a827daa7⟧
‹s1›1. Collect **paired observations**: rows where both A and B have non-empty values.
‹s2›2. Let `n` be the number of paired observations.
‹s3›‹s3.c1›3. If `n < 2`, ‹s3.c2›correlation is `null`.
‹s4›‹s4.c1›4. Compute paired means: `mean_a = sum(ai) / n`, ‹s4.c2›`mean_b = sum(bi) / n`.
‹s5›5. Compute `numerator = sum((ai - mean_a) * (bi - mean_b))`.
‹s6›6. Compute `denom = sqrt(sum((ai - mean_a)^2) * sum((bi - mean_b)^2))`.
‹s7›‹s7.c1›7. If `denom == 0` ‹s7.c2›(either column has zero variance in the paired set), ‹s7.c3›correlation is `null`.
‹s8›‹s8.c1›8. Otherwise, ‹s8.c2›`correlation = numerator / denom`.

⟦R2.S4.P4#a6bfaf8d⟧
‹s1›Each entry in the `correlations` array is:
‹s2›```json
{"column_a": "col1", "column_b": "col2", "correlation": 0.95}
```

⟦R2.S4.P5#fa445412⟧
‹s1›‹s1.c1›- `column_a`: the name of the first column ‹s1.c2›(earlier in header order).
‹s2›‹s2.c1›- `column_b`: the name of the second column ‹s2.c2›(later in header order).
‹s3›‹s3.c1›- `correlation`: the Pearson coefficient as a JSON number, ‹s3.c2›or `null` if undefined.
‹s4›‹s4.c1›- The array is sorted by `column_a` position in the header, ‹s4.c2›then by `column_b` position.
‹s5›‹s5.c1›- If there are fewer than 2 numeric columns, ‹s5.c2›`correlations` is an empty array.

⟦R2.S8#ce8855e5⟧ ### `deduplicate`

⟦R2.S8.P1#15068784⟧
Remove duplicate rows based on a set of key columns.

⟦R2.S8.P2#23ab1a98⟧
```json
{"op": "deduplicate", "columns": ["id", "name"], "keep": "first"}
```

⟦R2.S8.P3#112c2e7a⟧
‹s1›‹s1.c1›- `columns` ‹s1.c2›(optional array of strings): ‹s1.c3›column names to use for duplicate detection. If omitted or empty, ‹s1.c4›all columns are used.

‹s4›  - `"last"`: keep the last occurrence of each key combination.
‹s5›- Output preserves the relative order of retained rows as they appeared in the input.
‹s6›‹s6.c1›- If any column in `columns` does not exist, ‹s6.c2›exit with error: `ERROR: invalid recipe: column <name> not found`.

⟦R2.S9#31470ccf⟧ ### `split`

⟦R2.S9.P1#d1775e8a⟧

⟦R2.S13#2c622e97⟧ ### Fill `linear` strategy

⟦R2.S13.P1#c7f05473⟧
The existing `fill` transform now supports an additional strategy: `"linear"`.

⟦R2.S13.P2#b1266680⟧
```json
{"op": "fill", "columns": ["temperature"], "strategy": "linear"}
```

⟦R2.S13.P3#b5d0ff18⟧
For each empty cell in the specified columns:

⟦R2.S13.P4#1c9c3dad⟧
‹s1›‹s1.c1›1. Search upward ‹s1.c2›(decreasing row index) ‹s1.c3›for the nearest non-empty cell whose value parses as a float. Call this the **lower anchor** at index `lo` with value `v_lo`.
‹s2›‹s2.c1›2. Search downward ‹s2.c2›(increasing row index) ‹s2.c3›for the nearest non-empty cell whose value parses as a float. Call this the **upper anchor** at index `hi` with value `v_hi`.
‹s3›‹s3.c1›3. If **both** anchors are found, ‹s3.c2›interpolate: `result = v_lo + (v_hi - v_lo) * (i - lo) / (hi - lo)` where `i` is the current row index.
‹s4›‹s4.c1›4. If either anchor is **missing** ‹s4.c2›(no non-empty numeric value exists above or below), ‹s4.c3›the cell remains empty.
‹s5›‹s5.c1›5. Non-empty cells that do not parse as float are skipped during anchor search ‹s5.c2›(treated as if the cell were empty for interpolation purposes, but they are **not** themselves filled).

⟦R2.S13.P5#1937ab82⟧
**Output format:** interpolated values are formatted using Go's `strconv.FormatFloat(val, 'f', -1, 64)`.

⟦R2.S14.P3#7df5abec⟧
‹s1›‹s1.c1›- `column`: source column. If it does not exist, ‹s1.c2›exit with error: `ERROR: invalid recipe: column <name> not found`.

**`onehot`** method:

⟦R2.S14.P5#97228e33⟧
‹s1›‹s1.c1›1. Collect all unique non-empty values from `column`, ‹s1.c2›sorted ascending ‹s1.c3›(lexicographic).

**`ordinal`** method:

⟦R2.S14.P7#92e42d27⟧

⟦R2.S14.P8#cc16dfd3⟧
‹s1›‹s1.c1›1. Collect all unique non-empty values from `column`, ‹s1.c2›sorted ascending ‹s1.c3›(lexicographic).

⟦R2.S15#9e6b058e⟧ ### `rollup`

⟦R2.S15.P1#b0eefcf7⟧
‹s1.c1›Compute aggregations at multiple levels of a column hierarchy, ‹s1.c2›producing detail rows, ‹s1.c3›subtotals, ‹s1.c4›and a grand total.

⟦R2.S15.P2#0ccab21a⟧

```

⟦R2.S15.P3#39700597⟧
‹s1›‹s1.c1›- `columns`: array of grouping columns forming a hierarchy ‹s1.c2›(left to right = coarsest to finest).
‹s2›‹s2.c1›- `aggregations`: array of aggregation specs, ‹s2.c2›each with `column`, ‹s2.c3›`function`, ‹s2.c4›and `as`. Supported functions: `sum`, ‹s2.c5›`avg`, ‹s2.c6›`count`, ‹s2.c7›`min`, ‹s2.c8›`max` ‹s2.c9›(same semantics as the `aggregate` transform — non-numeric values skipped for `sum`/`avg`/`min`/`max`; `count` counts non-empty values; `avg` with zero numeric values yields `NaN`; `sum` with zero yields `0`; `min`/`max` with zero yield `NaN`).
‹s3›- If any column in `columns` or `aggregations[].column` does not exist: `ERROR: invalid recipe: column <name> not found`.

⟦R2.S15.P4#08adc5ec⟧
**Output:** The output header is the `columns` array followed by the `as` names from `aggregations`.

⟦R2.S15.P5#1af34882⟧
Output rows are produced at multiple hierarchy levels:

⟦R2.S15.P6#56a8de61⟧
‹s1›‹s1.c1›1. **Detail level** ‹s1.c2›(all grouping columns): ‹s1.c3›group by all columns in `columns`. Each unique combination produces one row with the actual group values and aggregation results.
‹s2›‹s2.c1›2. **Subtotal levels** ‹s2.c2›(from finest to coarsest): ‹s2.c3›for each level `k` from `len(columns)-1` down to `1`, ‹s2.c4›group by the first `k` columns. In each subtotal row, ‹s2.c5›columns at positions `k` through `len(columns)-1` have the value `"*"`.
‹s3›‹s3.c1›3. **Grand total** ‹s3.c2›(level 0): ‹s3.c3›a single row where all grouping columns have the value `"*"` and aggregations are computed over all rows.

⟦R2.S15.P7#61108cd4⟧
Row ordering:

⟦R2.S15.P8#cc3ec4db⟧
‹s1›‹s1.c1›1. Detail rows first, ‹s1.c2›sorted by the group column values in ascending lexicographic order ‹s1.c3›(left to right).
‹s2›‹s2.c1›2. Then subtotal rows for each level, ‹s2.c2›from the finest subtotal level ‹s2.c3›(grouping by all but the last column) ‹s2.c4›to the coarsest ‹s2.c5›(grouping by just the first column). ‹s2.c6›Within each subtotal level, ‹s2.c7›rows are sorted by the included group column values ascending.
‹s3›3. Grand total row last.

⟦R2.S16#c6d64bda⟧ ### `detect`

⟦R2.S16.P1#662e35be⟧
‹s1.c1›Detect outliers in a numeric column, ‹s1.c2›appending a new boolean column.

⟦R2.S16.P2#ff96b305⟧

{"op": "detect", "column": "value", "method": "iqr", "as": "is_outlier", "factor": 1.5}
```

⟦R2.S16.P3#e4713ede⟧
‹s1›‹s1.c1›- `column`: source column. Must exist, ‹s1.c2›otherwise: `ERROR: invalid recipe: column <name> not found`.
‹s2›‹s2.c1›- `method`: detection algorithm ‹s2.c2›(see below).
‹s3›‹s3.c1›- `as`: new column name, ‹s3.c2›appended as the last column.
‹s4›- `factor`: numeric threshold multiplier.

⟦R2.S16.P4#b4fc0ae2⟧
‹s1›‹s1.c1›First, ‹s1.c2›collect all non-empty values from `column` that parse as floats ‹s1.c3›(Go's `strconv.ParseFloat` with bit size 64). ‹s2›Compute detection thresholds from these values. ‹s3›‹s3.c1›Then, ‹s3.c2›for each row:

⟦R2.S16.P5#09ba5b3d⟧
‹s1›- If the cell is empty or does not parse as float: new column is `"0"`.
‹s2›‹s2.c1›- Otherwise, ‹s2.c2›apply the method's test. Result: `"1"` ‹s2.c3›(outlier) ‹s2.c4›or `"0"` ‹s2.c5›(not outlier).

⟦R2.S16.P6#3520a712⟧
**Methods:**

⟦R2.S16.P7#39eb155b⟧
‹s1.c1›- **`iqr`**: Compute Q1, ‹s1.c2›Q3 using the same percentile method as the `profile` command. IQR = Q3 - Q1. A value is an outlier if `value < Q1 - factor * IQR` or `value > Q3 + factor * IQR`. If fewer than 2 numeric values exist, ‹s1.c3›all get `"0"`.

⟦R2.S16.P8#bd240513⟧
‹s1.c1›- **`zscore`**: Compute population mean and population standard deviation ‹s1.c2›(same formulas as profile's `mean` and `stddev`). ‹s1.c3›A value is an outlier if `|value - mean| / stddev > factor`. If stddev is 0, ‹s1.c4›all values get `"0"`.

⟦R2.S16.P9#4ebe98f6⟧
‹s1.c1›- **`mad`**: Compute median of all numeric values. Compute MAD = median of `|xi - median|` for all numeric values. Compute modified Z-score for each value: `modified_z = 0.6745 * (value - median) / MAD`. A value is an outlier if `|modified_z| > factor`. If MAD is 0: values equal to the median get `"0"`, ‹s1.c2›values not equal to the median get `"1"`.

‹s4›‹s4.c1›- `as`: new column name, ‹s4.c2›appended as the last column.

⟦R2.S17.P4#a48449d1⟧
‹s1›‹s1.c1›First, ‹s1.c2›collect all non-empty values from `column` that parse as floats. ‹s2›Then for each row:

⟦R2.S17.P5#364d45cb⟧

**Methods:**

⟦R2.S17.P7#07250743⟧
‹s1›- **`width`**: Equal-width bins.
‹s2›  1. Compute `w = (max - min) / bins`.
‹s3›‹s3.c1›  2. Bin index for value `v`: `i = floor((v - min) / w)`, ‹s3.c2›clamped to `[0, bins - 1]`.

‹s1›- **`quantile`**: Equal-frequency bins using percentile boundaries.

‹s4›‹s4.c1›  3. Labels: same format as `width`, ‹s4.c2›using `boundary[i]` as `low` and `boundary[i+1]` as `high`. The last bin's `high` is `max`.

⟦R2.S19.P1#8b6cfbbd⟧

⟦R2.S19.P2#4b2a2c56⟧
‹s1.c1›Reads two CSV files and compares them row-by-row using the specified key columns, ‹s1.c2›producing a JSON diff report.

⟦R2.S20#6d602327⟧ ### Comparison logic

⟦R2.S20.P1#4282a676⟧
‹s1›‹s1.c1›1. Read both CSV files ‹s1.c2›(first row is header).
‹s2›‹s2.c1›2. Both files must have identical headers ‹s2.c2›(same column names in the same order). ‹s2.c3›If not, ‹s2.c4›exit with error: `ERROR: schema mismatch: headers differ`.
‹s3›3. The `--key` flag specifies a comma-separated list of column names that form the composite key.
‹s4›‹s4.c1›4. If any key column does not exist in the header, ‹s4.c2›exit with error: `ERROR: invalid key: column <name> not found`.
‹s5›‹s5.c1›5. Build a composite key for each row by joining the values of the key columns with a null byte ‹s5.c2›(`\x00`) ‹s5.c3›separator.
‹s6›6. Classify rows:
‹s7›   - **added**: key exists in right but not in left.
‹s8›   - **removed**: key exists in left but not in right.
‹s9›‹s9.c1›   - **modified**: key exists in both, ‹s9.c2›but at least one non-key column differs.
‹s10›‹s10.c1›   - Rows with matching keys and identical values in all columns are **unchanged** ‹s10.c2›(not included in changes).
‹s11›‹s11.c1›7. If the left file has duplicate keys, ‹s11.c2›only the first occurrence is used. Same for the right file.

⟦R2.S23#55d6a43c⟧ ### Changes ordering

⟦R2.S23.P1#c2a20049⟧
‹s1›The `changes` array is sorted by:
‹s2›‹s2.c1›1. Type order: `"added"` first, ‹s2.c2›then `"removed"`, ‹s2.c3›then `"modified"`.
‹s3›‹s3.c1›2. Within each type: sorted ascending by composite key ‹s3.c2›(lexicographic comparison of the joined key string).

⟦R2.S24#a612a442⟧ ### Error handling

⟦R2.S24.P1#5f04c9dc⟧
‹s1›‹s1.c1›- Missing left file: exit code 1, ‹s1.c2›stderr `ERROR: file not found: <path>`.
‹s2›‹s2.c1›- Missing right file: exit code 1, ‹s2.c2›stderr `ERROR: file not found: <path>`.
‹s3›‹s3.c1›- Missing `--key` flag: exit code 1, ‹s3.c2›stderr `ERROR: --key is required`.
‹s4›‹s4.c1›- Invalid key column: exit code 1, ‹s4.c2›stderr `ERROR: invalid key: column <name> not found`.
‹s5›‹s5.c1›- Schema mismatch: exit code 1, ‹s5.c2›stderr `ERROR: schema mismatch: headers differ`.
‹s6›‹s6.c1›- Missing `--output` flag: exit code 1, ‹s6.c2›stderr `ERROR: --output is required`.

⟦R2.S25#d984f585⟧ ### Extended compare flags

⟦R2.S25.P1#f1a2f4b4⟧
The `compare` command accepts two additional optional flags:

⟦R2.S25.P2#36842bf7⟧
‹s1.c1›**`--tolerance <number>`** ‹s1.c2›(default: `0`):

⟦R2.S25.P3#22cc5fd5⟧
‹s1›‹s1.c1›When comparing values between left and right rows for "modified" detection, ‹s1.c2›if both values parse as floats ‹s1.c3›(Go's `strconv.ParseFloat` with bit size 64) ‹s1.c4›and the absolute difference `|left_float - right_float| <= tolerance`, ‹s1.c5›the values are treated as equal. ‹s2›Non-numeric values or values where only one side parses as float use exact string comparison.

⟦R2.S25.P4#387660ad⟧
‹s1.c1›**`--ignore <col1,col2,...>`** ‹s1.c2›(optional):

⟦R2.S25.P5#b9c5e8c1⟧
‹s1›Comma-separated list of column names to exclude from change detection. ‹s2›‹s2.c1›These columns are still included in output row objects, ‹s2.c2›but differences in ignored columns do not cause a row to be classified as "modified". ‹s3›‹s3.c1›If all non-key, ‹s3.c2›non-ignored columns are equal, ‹s3.c3›the row is "unchanged". ‹s4›The `diff` array in "modified" entries does not include ignored columns.

⟦R2.S25.P6#755e9597⟧
‹s1.c1›- If any column in `--ignore` does not exist in the header: exit code 1, ‹s1.c2›stderr `ERROR: invalid ignore: column <name> not found`.

⟦R2.S26#3b44e225⟧ ### Formatting

⟦R2.S26.P1#c0b59a93⟧
Output uses JSON with 2-space indentation and a trailing newline.

⟦R2.S27#cabe366e⟧ ## New transforms (continued)

⟦R2.S28#339652e4⟧ ### `hash`

⟦R2.S28.P1#9b7106d3⟧
‹s1.c1›Compute a SHA-256 hash of specified columns for each row, ‹s1.c2›appending a new column with the hex digest.

⟦R2.S28.P2#290f17c4⟧
```json
{"op": "hash", "columns": ["id", "name", "value"], "as": "row_hash"}
```

⟦R2.S28.P3#410decc1⟧
‹s1›‹s1.c1›- `columns` ‹s1.c2›(array of strings): ‹s1.c3›column names whose values are included in the hash. If omitted or empty, ‹s1.c4›all columns are used ‹s1.c5›(in header order).
‹s2›‹s2.c1›- `as` ‹s2.c2›(string): ‹s2.c3›name for the new column, ‹s2.c4›appended as the last column in the header.

⟦R2.S28.P4#30514ee5⟧
**Computation:**

⟦R2.S28.P5#dc2ce3cf⟧
‹s1.c1›For each row, ‹s1.c2›concatenate the values of the specified columns separated by a null byte ‹s1.c3›(`\x00`), ‹s1.c4›compute the SHA-256 digest, ‹s1.c5›and format as a 64-character lowercase hexadecimal string.

⟦R2.S28.P6#9bdff454⟧
‹s1.c1›Example: for columns `["id", "name"]` and values `["1", "Alice"]`, ‹s1.c2›the hash input is the byte string `1\x00Alice` ‹s1.c3›(5 bytes with `\x00` as the separator byte).

⟦R2.S28.P7#9b68fe86⟧
‹s1›‹s1.c1›- Empty cell values are included as empty strings ‹s1.c2›(contributing only the separator).
‹s2›‹s2.c1›- If any column in `columns` does not exist, ‹s2.c2›exit with error: `ERROR: invalid recipe: column <name> not found`.
